analysis.one_liner: Gave patients the right to see, correct, and control who sees their medical records, with criminal and civil penalties for misuse.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to two subcommittees in 1999; it never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given every patient the right to inspect and copy their own medical records, to add corrections, and to decide who may see their health information. It would have barred hospitals, insurers, employers, and others from disclosing medical details without written permission, required security safeguards for electronic records, and set criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison and civil fines for wrongful disclosure. Congress had set itself a deadline of August 1999 to pass a medical privacy law; this bill was one answer, but it never moved past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who sees a doctor, holds insurance, or works for an employer with a health plan. Patients could get their records within 15 business days, add their own supplements to disputed records, require separate consent before information was shared for non-treatment purposes, sue for violations, and be shielded from retaliation.

how_it_helps.text: Requires health care providers, health plans, employers, insurers, schools, and universities to let individuals inspect and copy their own protected health information within 15 business days, and to add supplements to records they dispute.

Prohibits those parties from using or disclosing protected health information except as authorized, with disclosure limited to the minimum necessary, and bars conditioning treatment or payment on consent to unrelated disclosures.

Creates an Office of Health Information Privacy at HHS to receive and investigate complaints and conduct audits, and imposes criminal penalties up to $500,000 and 10 years in prison for wrongful disclosure for commercial gain, plus civil penalties and a private right of action with attorney's fees.

Requires safeguards for electronic records, a 7-year accounting of disclosures not related to payment or treatment, notice of privacy practices, and protection against retaliation for exercising these rights.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, employers, life insurers, providers, researchers, and schools that hold health records would bear compliance costs for notices, authorizations, safeguards, and disclosure records, and would lose the ability to freely share or commercialize identifiable patient data.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is broad: nearly every entity touching health records—from small provider offices to employers and universities—must build authorization systems, safeguards, and 7-year disclosure logs, and the bill's civil penalties reach up to $100,000 for a general business practice.

The private right of action, allowing individuals to recover compensatory and punitive damages plus attorney's fees for knowing or negligent violations, could expose health care and insurance entities to significant litigation cost.

Even supporters acknowledged tradeoffs: the bill creates a regime of consent, segregation, and court-order requirements for law enforcement and judicial access to records that could slow investigations and litigation, and it defers key research-consent decisions to later HHS rulemaking rather than resolving them in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to every patient: control over who sees their most sensitive information, at a time when the bill itself found that the traditional doctor-patient confidence was at risk as records went electronic. The costs are real but ordinary regulatory costs—compliance spending and more constrained data sharing for insurers, employers, and providers—with explicit carve-outs for treatment, payment, public health, emergencies, and oversight. The main design weakness is that it punts the hardest question, research consent, to a future HHS study. On balance the protections for individuals outweigh the compliance burden, which is why the outcome matters more than the drafting.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to the Commerce and Judiciary committees, which sent it down to subcommittees; it sat there for the rest of the Congress without a hearing or a vote and expired when the session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the Medical Information Privacy and Security Act on March 10, 1999, joined by 21 original cosponsors.

The bill's findings cite HIPAA's directive that Congress enact health privacy legislation before August 21, 1999, and state that the traditional confidentiality between patient and provider was at risk as records moved into computer systems.
The House referred the bill to the Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
On March 30, 1999 it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment; on September 24, 1999 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution.
No further action was taken: the bill was never reported out of committee, never debated, and never received a vote in either chamber before the 106th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Entities that hold, share, and profit from Americans' health records—insurers, employers, and health data handlers—went on without a binding federal consent-and-enforcement regime, while patients gained no new rights.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies holding and sharing health data

for.name: Rep. Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 21 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 46 House Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, bringing the bill's backing to 48 House members.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and sent the bill to its Health and Environment Subcommittee; the committee never reported it out.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received a split referral for provisions in its jurisdiction and sent the bill to its Constitution Subcommittee; the committee never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 47 cosponsors were Democrats or allied Independents; no House Republican sponsored the bill, and the committees that buried it never recorded a vote.

industries.note: The bill restricted how insurers could use and disclose enrollees' health records, required informed written authorizations, and exposed them to civil penalties and debarment from federal health programs for violations. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against patients' control over their own records.

Employers offering health plans were covered parties: they could not route employee health information to people making personnel decisions without separate authorization and could not condition employment on consent. This closed a channel employers had used to see workers' medical details.

Providers faced compliance duties—notices, authorizations, safeguards, disclosure logs—but gained the restoration of patient trust the bill's findings said was eroding, which the bill argued affects patients' willingness to seek care.

Life insurers were among the specifically covered parties and would have needed authorization for use of applicants' and policyholders' protected health information, limiting access to underwriting data.

The bill extended federal human-subjects protections to all health research using identifiable data and required eventual rules on informed consent, while preserving pathways for research on de-identified data and reporting to Congress on the tradeoffs.
